accuracy.evidence: Coin facts checked against The Royal Mint specifications: 1p 20.3 mm and 2p 25.9 mm (copper-plated steel), 5p 18.0 mm and 10p 24.5 mm (nickel-plated steel, round), 20p 21.4 mm and 50p 27.3 mm (seven-sided, cupro-nickel), £1 23.43 mm (12-sided, gold-coloured outer ring and silver-coloured centre) and £2 28.4 mm (gold-coloured ring, silver-coloured centre). The lab draws every coin at its real relative diameter, so each size trap (2p wider than 5p, 10p wider than 20p, 50p wider than £1, 1p wider than 5p) is true to life. £5 and £10 note colours follow the Bank of England polymer notes. Parameterised answers a, 2*a and a are whole numbers at every corner.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the slips NCETM lists for Year 1 money: bigger coin is worth more (four size-trap pairs in the 'Which is worth more?' scene with the reason naming both sizes, robot saying 1, p3, m6, challenge 'size'), more coins means more money (robot saying 3, p5, challenge 'many'), £1 read as 1 and so less than 50p (the 50p v £1 pair, robot saying 5, m3, challenge 'pound') and coins of equal value seen as different (the swap scene and its predict, m1, m2, challenge 'count').

lab_distinct.evidence: The lab is about recognising coins and their value, with coins drawn at true relative size and shape (7-sided 20p and 50p, 12-sided two-colour £1): find a coin by its number among four, pick the coin worth more when the bigger coin is worth less, tap coins into slots from least to most, and fill a tray with 1p, 2p or 10p coins until it equals one coin. flagcoin (688, ages 7-8) pays amounts, counts up for change and uses bar models; it never orders coins or tests size against value. The lab_distinct gate keeps flag_coinval.js under 30% similar to every lab.

lab_teaches.evidence: The child learns by doing: in the swap scene the tray total ticks up with each coin tapped in ('6 × 1p = 6p'), turns green at exactly 10p and red with 'Too much' if they overfill, so they see ten 1p coins equal one 10p. In the pairs scene a wrong tap on the big coin gets 'The 2p is bigger, but it is worth less. 5 is more than 2', so size versus number is stated at the moment of the slip. Line-up only accepts the least valuable coin left and says which coin is worth less.

predictions.evidence: Two predictions aimed at misconceptions: 'Which is worth more: the big 2p or the small 5p?' (tempting answer: the big 2p) before the size-trap pairs, and 'Which is more money: one 10p coin, or ten 1p coins?' (tempting answer: ten 1p coins) before the swap scene where the tray of ten 1p coins matches one 10p. The step completion message reveals the child's own prediction.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six rotating challenge questions, each with two tagged wrong answers. why() has six distinct messages: size (size does not tell you the value), same (they are not the same, compare the numbers), count (ten 1p coins make 10p), many (one 20p beats three 1p coins), look (the 20p and 50p have 7 flat sides) and pound (£1 is 100 pence). Each names the slip and gives the fix in short words.

readability.evidence: Kid text uses short sentences and everyday words (coin, note, worth, big, number) and reads well under the family kid FK limit; the adult text names coin, note, value, penny, pence and pound and passes the adult limit. On the canvas, coin labels are dark on light copper, silver or gold faces and signs shrink to fit at 360 px.

no_filler.evidence: Each kid paragraph teaches one idea: coins and notes carry their value, the list of UK coins with p and £, size versus value with the 2p and 5p, and swapping one coin for many plus £1 = 100p. The adult text gives the Year 1 requirement, key words, how to tell coins apart by colour and shape, three named mistakes with what to do, and what the lab does. The content gate found no filler and under 12% overlap with every other lesson.

mobile.evidence: Checked iPhone 13 screenshots of every step in dark theme and desktop in light theme, at rest and part-way through each Show me: the four coins sit in a 2 x 2 grid of tap cells about 170 x 120 px, the pairs scene uses two half-width cells, the line-up row has four slot boxes under the coins, and the swap tray fills with up to ten coins in two rows next to the big coin, with a wide 'Tap to add a 1p' pile. Every canvas action has a big button twin under the canvas.

accessibility.evidence: Every canvas action has a labelled button: each coin in the find, pairs and line-up scenes (named in words, e.g. 'Find the 10p: tap 2 pence'), Add a coin and Take one out, and Right or Slip. The tray total and every result are spoken through c.say and the canvas aria-label after each change; challenge feedback is a polite live region. Coins are told apart by their printed number, not colour alone. The walk gate's axe run is clean in both themes on desktop and iPhone 13.
